title: DNS: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and TXT records and recursive resolution

videos.script: Every connection in the last three lessons went to an address: 192.0.2.80. Nobody types that. People type www.example.com, and something has to turn the name into the number before a single packet can leave. {{names}} That something is DNS, the Domain Name System. It is a huge distributed database, split so that nobody holds all of it, and it answers billions of questions a day, most of them from a cache. {{dns}} In this lesson you will ask DNS questions with dig and read every part of the answer. You will follow one name from the root, through .com, to the server that actually knows it. {{walk}} You will change a record and watch the world keep the old answer for exactly as long as it was told to. That is what people call propagation. {{ttl}} And you will see the four ways a DNS answer can go wrong, each with its own name, and the hosts file that quietly overrides all of it. {{fail}} The DNS here is the lab's own, with its own root. The names are the ones reserved for examples, and every answer came from the servers in the drawing. {{honest}}
